newsitem.title: USA: Spicy salsas continue to burn up U.S. market.
newsitem.headline: Spicy salsas continue to burn up U.S. market.

text.p: The raging popularity of spicy salsa, which soared past ketchup as America's favourite condiment two years ago, is showing no signs of cooling off.
Industry leaders gathered here this weekend for the world's largest trade show for hot and spicy foods said sales trends indicate no end to the meteoric growth seen over the past decade.

"This has grown beyond our wildest dreams," said Dave DeWitt, who started the National Fiery Foods trade show in 1988 with only 38 exhibitors and has watched the number grow to more than 250 this year. "The expansion proves how fast the fiery foods industry is growing."

The statistic bear out his claim. Farm production of chili of all types in the United States rose by almost 600 percent from 19 million pounds in 1970 to 130 million pounds in 1995, the last full year for which the numbers are available.

Retail sales of condiments, including barbecue sauces, ketchup and hot pepper sauces, nearly doubled from $362 million in 1988 to an estimated $670 million this year, fuelled primarily by the rise in salsa sales.

"We see no limits to the growth of this industry," said Kenn Livingston of Paw Paw, Mich., who was hawking his company's Mean Devil Woman Cajun Pepper Sauce at the trade show in Albuquerque. "There are closet pepperheads all over the north. They've just been waiting to come out.'

Livingston said that, until two years ago, Michigan had no stores specialising in chili products but that he has since introduced two "hot shops" and a Cajun restaurant in Three Rivers, while two other Cajun restaurants have also opened up in the same area.
His restaurant -- called "Cajun Radar's Road Kill Restaurant and Deli: Where Flat Food Comes Alive" -- is booming. "We can't keep the shelves stocked in the store inside our restaurant," he said.

The scores of tortured tongues and sweating brows here Sunday were a sure sign that the 6,000 chili lovers attending the last day of the show were once again pursuing their passion for pain with great relish.

"This may hurt for a minute or so, but after that you feel nothing but pleasure," said David Taylor of Lubbock, Texas, spooning up a corn tortilla chip with a small amount of his Screaming Sphincter Habanero Salsa. "Once people get used to the pain, they can't get enough," he said.

More than 12,000 people attended the Fiery Foods show this weekend to sample new products, watch cooking demonstrations from renowned chili chefs and, on occasion, scramble to find a cold beer or soda to douse a flaming mouth.

Carin Froelich of Ingelby Farms Inc. in Dublin, Pa., said her firm's Heinie-Hurtin' Hot Sauce is pioneering a new chili -- the lemon-drop habanero -- which was developed in secret by Amish researchers who crossed a citrus seed with the hottest of hot chiles, the habanero.

"We can't really mass produce it until we get enough seeds but we have developed a loyal following in the northeast," said Froelich, who was busy Sunday selling salsas, jams, oils, vinegars and salad dressings laced with the new chili.
There were some sceptics at the show, however.
"Let's face it, there is only so much you can do with chili," said Fred Bonavita of San Antonio, Texas, who stopped in to see the show while vacationing with his wife.
"I don't really see anything new here," he said. "It looks like things may have peaked."

But DeWitt, an acknowledged world expert on all things hot and spicy, who publishes a bimonthly industry publication and has an internet site for "chili-heads," said he sees no cause for concern as he took a mouthful of serrano chili salsa.
"It's been a frantic year and I don't see things slowing down any time soon," he said, wiping beads of sweat from his forehead.
